mission: Aftermath of Iressa’s death. Talon presses Ben about the option he refused. Ben cannot cleanly answer whether it would have worked. While they process the loss, they examine Iressa’s dying transmission and find what she actually sent: a documentary reconstruction tying the Foundation, Korda, and the Iresh thread together — and the strategic revelation about the holocron’s identity-shaping purpose. Ben does the correct thing first. He holo-calls Luke at Shedu Maad. Luke listens, asks his quiet careful questions, and tells Ben that this needs to go to Saba. Ben then holo-calls Saba Sebatyne, Grand Master. Saba listens with Barabel gravity, asks her own sharp questions, and tells Ben the Order will review the case properly. He should return to Shedu Maad in person and bring the documentary chain to the Council. The review will be careful. It will take time. Ben hangs up the call and looks at Talon. They both know what Saba’s “review” means in the timeframe they have. The Vigil is already moving on Iresh. The institutional path, even with Luke and Saba’s full support, is going to be too slow. This is the moment Ben pivots. He decides to keep building the documentary case from Iressa’s tools and notes while preparing to act outside official channels. He is no longer waiting for the Order to validate his findings. He is going to Iresh — if he can get there in time and the evidence holds, the Council can ratify what he did afterward. If he is wrong, he answers for it. Either way, waiting is no longer an option. The Midpoint reversal: Ben stops reacting and starts moving. He goes on offense.
why_now: Chapter 16 occupies the midpoint phase and carries the next locked outline turn.
conflict: Iressa’s death proves restraint can cost lives. The Midpoint should land as both emotional cost and strategic clarity. Ben’s decision should feel like the moment he stops being a victim of the past and starts acting on it — even when the method carries danger. The two holo calls (Luke, Saba) should establish that Ben tried the right way first. The institutional path is not refused out of arrogance; it is refused after being tried. Saba is not the villain. The slowness is. Reader-onboarding / clarity note: Plain-language consequence: Iressa died protecting the clue. The clue tells them the enemy is already on Iresh and tells them why it matters (identity-shaping). The Order will review the case properly, which means weeks Ben does not have. He chooses to keep building evidence and prepare to move on Iresh himself. Continuity / craft notes: - This is Pinch Point 1’s emotional aftermath and the Midpoint structural pivot, in the same chapter. - The drafter should not let the holo calls become exposition. They are short. Luke’s call is paternal; Saba’s call is institutional. Both end with Ben understanding the cost of doing things the right way. - Ben’s decision should be quiet, not declamatory. He does not announce it. He simply starts working on what comes next. Talon notices and follows.
turning_point: Ben and Talon relocate operations to Iressa’s secondary cache and begin assembling what they need to move on Iresh themselves. The story has shifted from investigation to active disruption.
closing_hook: Ben and Talon relocate operations to Iressa’s secondary cache and begin assembling what they need to move on Iresh themselves. The story has shifted from investigation to active disruption.
setting: Coruscant, Iressa's secondary cache — a quiet leased basement workshop in the warehouse district she had maintained for years, separate from Civitas and from her residence. Old terminals, hand-labelled crates of datachips, the smell of soldering paste. Ben and Talon work here for several days after the archive disaster. Two short holocalls (Luke first, then Saba) happen from this room.
